title: Zhu Xiaohu Changes His Tune: DeepSeek Has Him Almost Believing in AGI
dek: A year ago he said he would never invest in any Chinese large-model company; now he says if Liang Wenfeng opens a round, "I would definitely invest" — price no longer matters much, what matters is being part of witnessing the emergence of human AGI and AI consciousness.
why: Zhu Xiaohu's complete turn within a year from "not bullish on large models" to "almost believing in AGI," including his specific judgments on closed source, data flywheels, Agents, and Stargate — high information density.
who: Founders and investors watching startup opportunities in China's AI application layer, especially teams still agonizing over whether to keep building their own foundation models, or trying to judge where the open-source ecosystem is heading.
skip: After 54:26, the parts about Hangzhou, investment ratios, and the quick-fire Q&A are lower in information density and can be skipped.

points.h: For the leader, open source is a curse — open too late and it's pointless
points.body: Zhu Xiaohu classifies OpenAI's flip-flopping on open source as "the leader's curse": when you're ahead you definitely want to keep it closed, and once others catch up, open-sourcing is hard. The mechanism he gives is cost — you spent ten times the cost to develop the foundation model, and a Chinese company catches up at one-tenth the cost in at most twelve months, so whether to still pour that money in today is a test even for America's big tech firms, even for VCs. So he judges that OpenAI will not open-source, because open-sourcing is also too late: programmers worldwide are already building on DeepSeek's open-source architecture, and open-sourcing again "wouldn't mean much."

points.h: 20 days to 20 million DAU, without spending a cent on ads
points.body: Zhu Xiaohu says DeepSeek is "the Android of the AI era has already appeared," because its growth speed is unprecedented: 20 days to 20 million DAU, and without spending a single cent on advertising — unlike many domestic companies that burn money on投放, it relies entirely on word of mouth. He repeatedly stresses that its writing's "beauty and depth" astonishes users, and that he himself uses it every day to ask relatively deep, relatively hard questions, to see whether its feedback can offer insight. This point is the factual foundation for all the judgments that follow — the value of closed source, the reshaping of valuations, the explosion of applications.

points.h: Compute and algorithms aren't the bottleneck — high-quality data is
points.body: Zhu Xiaohu says a hundred-thousand-card cluster trained for six or seven months and the result was "probably indeed quite ordinary," so the demands on compute and algorithms are not that high now; the core is high-quality data. He uses a chef analogy: what corpus you train on and what the parameter weights are determine the dish you produce — some are Sichuan cuisine, some Cantonese. He speculates that DeepSeek's beautiful writing and profound answers in philosophy and quantum mechanics may be this team's genes — they enjoy these kinds of thinking, so the training corpus is higher quality in these areas. He also mentions that the initial corpus needs PhD-level, domain-expert-level people to label it.

points.h: The data flywheel isn't worth much — his biggest lesson in two years
points.body: Zhu Xiaohu says this is his biggest lesson in the past two years: he used to think the biggest moat in this wave of AI might be the data flywheel, but now it seems — including for DeepSeek, including OpenAI's own research — the data flywheel isn't worth much. The mechanism is that most user data is repetitive, low-information, meaningless; idle chat doesn't produce intelligence. What truly has flywheel value is high-quality data that requires professionals from various industries to label. So the moat shifts to occupying user mindshare, building customer relationships, and workflow integration — acquiring 20 million users in 20 days without spending on advertising is itself a very large moat.

points.h: Closed-source models are clearly not worth that much money anymore
points.body: Zhu Xiaohu says the entire LLM industry needs to reshape its valuation system, because closed-source models are clearly not worth that much money anymore, especially America's OpenAI — if a hundred-thousand-card cluster brings no further breakthrough and it's only optimizing inference, then domestic players will catch up quickly, and the valuation definitely can't hold. On the Stargate project Trump announced, he thinks that still believes in the old Scaling Law, the era of compute is king, whereas today compute isn't that big a bottleneck, algorithms aren't a bottleneck either, and what matters more is professional data in various domains, so that investment "is meaningless," plus Elon Musk and the others don't actually have that much money — it's a show performed for Trump.

points.h: In China, you can assume the foundation model is free
points.body: Zhu Xiaohu's advice to AI founders is even more firm than a year ago: any startup must absolutely not research foundation models, especially in China — you can assume the foundation model is free, and its capabilities are already strong enough, so just look at what users actually need on top of it, grasp the need, and provide the best solution. He gives the example of call centers — take over the entire call center, no matter how much is done by humans and how much by AI, and directly offer the client half the current price. He also reiterates his AIGC PMF view: the model is already this powerful, and if 10 people can't find PMF, 100 people certainly can't.

points.h: Even if ByteDance switches to open source now, catching up won't be easy
points.body: Asked whether ByteDance could still catch up if it pushed hard, Zhu Xiaohu says "it won't be easy for them either," and switching to open source right away isn't easy either. The mechanism is that when a big company does open source, unless it's as thorough as DeepSeek, if it opens up like Llama — not that thorough — others still can't use it, and may prefer to use DeepSeek. So he judges that the most important thing for DeepSeek is to keep moving forward, keep catching up to OpenAI, and establish its lead and open-source ecosystem, so that it will be very hard for big companies to catch up later. He also suggests that this year we may see Tongyi Qianwen make its ecosystem compatible with DeepSeek, which he thinks would be a more meaningful landmark event.

points.h: An Agent is just a program — don't be fooled by definitions
points.body: On OpenAI's five technical levels from L1 to L5, Zhu Xiaohu says "actually it's just another definition," and an Agent is actually no different from an ordinary program — it's just that you communicate with it and have it arrange tasks for you. He thinks the core is still whether it can truly replace 50%, 80%, 90% of people in certain scenarios, truly without human intervention — that's the most core milestone. The progress he gives: programming went from maybe 30% last year to 50%, 70%, 80% this year, because the rules are relatively clear; more important is to look at domains where the rules aren't so clear, such as medicine, where people have already used OpenAI's Deep Research to write two papers and felt it wrote very well.

terms.def: The rule that model performance improves as compute, data, and parameter scale grow.
A training method that lets models improve themselves through reward signals; DeepSeek used it to boost capability at low cost.
The number of users who actually use a product each day.
A product finding a real market need that users are willing to keep using it for.
Corporate spending on long-term assets such as compute and equipment.

facts.k: Training duration of a hundred-thousand-card cluster
facts.v: About six or seven months, with no obvious performance improvement

facts.k: Cost for Chinese companies to catch up
facts.v: At most twelve months later, at one-tenth the cost

facts.k: Cards needed for a multimodal vision model
facts.v: One to two thousand cards are enough to train it

facts.k: Lifetime price of the Tongyi Qianwen AI hardware package

quotes.text: The data flywheel isn't worth much, because most user data is repetitive, low-information, meaningless.
For any startup, absolutely don't research foundation models — especially in China, you can assume the foundation model is free.
